title: Newton, Leibniz and the War Over Calculus
text:
Isaac Newton worked out his method of "fluxions," the core of calculus, in the 1660s but published little of it for decades. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed his own version independently in the 1670s and published it first, in 1684, with a notation so convenient that much of it is still used today.

For years the two were polite. Then, around 1699, followers of Newton began to hint that Leibniz had stolen the idea after seeing Newton's papers. Leibniz's supporters answered with hints of their own. In 1711 Leibniz appealed to the Royal Society in London to clear his name.

Newton was President of the Royal Society. He appointed a committee, supplied the documents and secretly wrote much of its report himself. In 1712 the Society published it as the Commercium Epistolicum, which found in Newton's favor. Newton then reviewed it anonymously, praising its conclusions. Leibniz died in 1716, largely neglected.

Historians now agree that both men discovered calculus independently. The feud split European mathematics: British mathematicians clung to Newton's notation out of loyalty and fell behind the Continent for about a century.
lesson: A feud over credit can damage not just the rivals but everyone around them. When you have real power in a dispute, use it fairly, not to judge your own case.
source: Royal Society, Commercium Epistolicum (1712); A. Rupert Hall, Philosophers at War (1980)
